legal_004:n1.prompt:
You are helping me draft the initial legal documents for our SaaS product: a Subscription/SaaS Agreement, Terms of Service, and Privacy Policy. Before drafting, ask me for any of the following if not already known: company legal name and jurisdiction of incorporation, product/service name and domain, governing law/venue for disputes, subscription pricing model (monthly/annual, tiers), payment terms, SLA/uptime commitment (if any), data types collected from users, any third-party data processors or subprocessors we use, support contact email, and the effective date to use.

Using this information, draft three separate documents in plain, standard commercial language: (1) a SaaS Subscription Agreement covering scope of service, fees and payment, term and termination, limitation of liability, warranties/disclaimers, IP ownership, confidentiality, and governing law; (2) a Terms of Service covering acceptable use, account responsibilities, service changes, and termination rights; (3) a Privacy Policy covering what data is collected, how it's used, storage/retention, third-party sharing, user rights, and contact information for privacy inquiries. Base these on widely accepted SaaS industry templates and structure, clearly labeling any clause that is a placeholder or assumption (e.g., liability caps, notice periods) so it can be reviewed.

Save the three drafts as separate clearly named files (e.g., saas_agreement_draft, terms_of_service_draft, privacy_policy_draft) and prepare a short summary listing key terms chosen, any assumptions made, and any open questions requiring legal input (e.g., liability cap amount, dispute jurisdiction).

Do not finalize, publish, or send these documents anywhere. Once drafts and the summary are ready, present them to me and stop for human sign-off before any changes are applied or documents are used externally.

legal_004:n2.prompt:
You are helping me draft a Terms of Service (ToS) document for our SaaS product as part of finalizing our SaaS subscription agreement package. Before drafting, ask me for any details you need that aren't already known, such as: our company/legal entity name, the product/service name, our domain (for hosting the ToS page), our jurisdiction/governing law, customer support contact email, whether we serve consumers or businesses (B2B vs B2C), any acceptable use restrictions specific to our product, subscription/billing terms (trial periods, auto-renewal, refund policy), limitation of liability preferences, and any third-party services or data processing we should disclose (e.g., payment processor, analytics tools).

Using this information, draft a complete, plain-language Terms of Service covering: acceptance of terms, description of service, account registration and eligibility, subscription fees and billing, acceptable use policy, intellectual property rights, user content/data ownership, termination rights, disclaimers and limitation of liability, indemnification, dispute resolution and governing law, and modification of terms. Keep the tone professional but readable, and flag any clauses that typically require attorney review (e.g., liability caps, arbitration clauses).

Produce the draft as a clean, well-formatted document (Markdown or plain text) ready for legal and stakeholder review. Do not publish, embed, or link it live anywhere, and do not treat this draft as final or legally binding. Since a human must explicitly approve before this is applied, stop for human sign-off once the draft is complete. Report back with the full draft text, a short summary of key terms chosen, and a list of open questions or clauses needing legal counsel input.

legal_004:n3.prompt:
You are helping me draft a Privacy Policy for my SaaS product as part of finalizing our legal agreements (subscription agreement, terms of service, and privacy policy).

Before starting, ask me for any of the following if not already provided: (1) my company legal name and jurisdiction of incorporation, (2) my product/domain name and website URL, (3) what categories of personal data we collect (e.g., account info, usage data, payment data, cookies/analytics), (4) which third-party processors or subprocessors we use (e.g., hosting provider, payment processor, analytics/email tools) and their general purpose, (5) whether we serve users in regions with specific privacy laws (GDPR/EEA, CCPA/California, or others) requiring tailored clauses, (6) our data retention practices, and (7) a contact email or address for privacy inquiries and data subject requests.

Using this information, draft a complete, plain-language Privacy Policy covering: what data is collected and how; purposes of processing; legal bases (if applicable); data sharing with processors/subprocessors; international data transfers (if relevant); data retention periods; user rights (access, deletion, correction, opt-out) and how to exercise them; cookie/tracking disclosures; children's privacy statement; security measures (described generally, not as guarantees); breach notification approach; policy update process; and contact details.

Format the draft clearly with numbered sections and plain-language explanations suitable for both legal review and end users. Flag any sections where you made assumptions or need clarification (e.g., specific processor names, retention periods) so I can confirm or correct them.

When the draft is complete, present it to me in full along with a short summary of key assumptions and open questions, then stop for human sign-off — do not publish, submit, or treat the policy as final without my explicit approval.

legal_004:n4.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for legal counsel review of our SaaS subscription agreement, terms of service, and privacy policy (step legal_004:n4). This is a policy-gate step: you must prepare everything but a human (our legal counsel) must explicitly approve before any changes are applied — you may not approve, sign, or submit anything on my behalf.

First, ask me for anything missing: our company/domain name, the current drafts (or their file locations) of the SaaS agreement, ToS, and privacy policy, the name/contact of the reviewing counsel, and any known deadline.

Then do the following:
1. Consolidate the three documents into a single review package with version labels and dates.
2. Draft a cover memo summarizing: purpose of each document, key commercial terms (pricing, term length, liability caps, termination), and any open questions or risk areas you notice (e.g., unclear data processing terms, missing indemnification language).
3. Prepare a checklist of specific items for counsel to confirm or flag (e.g., liability limitation adequacy, compliance with applicable privacy law, dispute resolution clause).
4. Draft an email to the reviewing counsel attaching/linking the package, requesting their review and explicit sign-off, with a suggested response deadline.
5. Set up a way to track the review status (e.g., a shared doc or tracker entry marked 'pending counsel review').

Do not send the email or make any changes to the documents based on assumed approval. Once your package and email draft are ready, stop for human sign-off — present the draft materials to me for review and confirm counsel has been asked to approve. When counsel's decision arrives, note that this is an async step: I will need to poll/check back with counsel for their response, and you should ask me to confirm the outcome (approved / changes requested) before any next step proceeds. Report back with the package summary, draft email, checklist, and current review status.

legal_004:n5.prompt:
You are helping me prepare to publish our attorney-approved SaaS Subscription Agreement, Terms of Service, and Privacy Policy to our live website. Do NOT publish or make anything live — this step requires my explicit sign-off before changes go live.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available: (1) the final approved text/documents for each of the three policies, (2) my website domain and which CMS or website platform we use (e.g., WordPress, Webflow, Squarespace, custom site) and confirmation I have configured credentials for it, (3) the target URLs/page slugs where each document should live (e.g., /terms, /privacy, /subscription-agreement), and (4) any footer/nav links that need to point to these pages.

Once you have the inputs, do the following: (a) prepare the exact page content for each of the three documents, formatted for the target CMS (headings, paragraphs, links) without altering the approved legal wording; (b) stage these as draft/unpublished pages in the CMS using my configured credentials, at the specified URLs; (c) prepare a side-by-side comparison checklist showing the staged draft text against the attorney-approved source text for each document, flagging any formatting differences (e.g., missing sections, truncated text, broken links); (d) draft the internal navigation/footer link updates as a proposed change list, but do not apply them live.

When finished, report back with: the staged draft URLs (or draft/preview links) for all three documents, the comparison checklist confirming text matches the approved source, and a summary of any discrepancies found. Then stop for human sign-off — I will personally verify the staged content against counsel's approved version and give the go-ahead before you publish anything live.
